question: Public administrations in EU countries, the EU institutions and European businesses have transferred an increasing number of their information systems and digital services to the cloud. It is estimated that a large number of the cloud services in use in Europe are controlled by US tech companies. Most operating systems have also been purchased from those companies.

This is not just a question of market position or cost-effectiveness, but of the European Union’s digital sovereignty. US cloud services companies are bound by US national legislation. This can sometimes put the EU’s principles of data protection and legal autonomy at odds with the legislation of a third country.

Cloud services can be used to host functions that are critical for society, such as core public administration information systems, social and healthcare data, and electoral registers. Digital infrastructure is comparable to energy, transport and communications networks, all of which require strategic autonomy. In the light of the foregoing, I put the following questions to the Commission: 1.
Should the EU build common, fully European cloud and data infrastructure that would enable public administration and critical functions to be independent of third-country legislation?

Does the Commission have any estimates of how much the EU institutions, EU programmes and the public sector in the Member States pay US cloud services companies each year, and how those cash flows affect Europe’s strategic autonomy and industrial competitiveness?

What practical steps does the Commission intend to take to develop European cloud services, open technologies and publicly owned or controlled digital infrastructure in order to reduce the EU’s dependence on individual non-EU operators?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) The Commission will present a proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act. This will facilitate the development and adoption of European cloud and AI technologies, especially in the public sector, thus addressing the risks stemming from the EU’s reliance on third countries.

The Act will promote the development of the EU cloud and AI offer by driving investment and simplifying permitting procedures, with the aim of tripling EU data centre capacity by 2030 and bringing it to a level that matches its needs by 2035.
The Act will provide a harmonised definition of sovereign cloud and AI computing services and criteria for the public sector to procure secure and sovereign services for the most critical use cases.

The intervention rationale is based on the report ‘The future of European competitiveness’, which estimates the European infrastructure investment gap to be around EUR 75 billion until 2030 and around 70% of the European cloud and AI market is dominated by US hyperscalers.

These figures illustrate the EU’s reliance on third countries for cloud and AI computing services and the risks to its strategic autonomy and industrial competitiveness. Leading by example, the Commission launched in 2025 a EUR 180 million tender for the provision of sovereign cloud services.

There are no global figures on how much the EU institutions, EU programmes or the national public sector pay for US cloud services companies, but in 2025, EU institutions, bodies and agencies spent EUR 87 million on public cloud services.
